content: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides specific recommendations for the management of anogenital ulcers and anorectal discharge, as well as guidelines for addressing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) globally. Below is a detailed explanation of these recommendations and their implications: Management of Anogenital Ulcers 1. Syndromic Treatment for Syphilis and Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV): WHO recommends treating patients for both syphilis and HSV on the same day when anogenital ulcers are present. 2. Targeted Treatment Based on Clinical Presentation: If the ulcer is recurrent or vesicular, treatment should focus on HSV. If the patient has no history of syphilis treatment in the past three months, treatment for syphilis should also be initiated. 3. Understanding Genital Ulcer Disease: Genital ulcers are breaks in the skin or mucosa that may appear as sores, ulcers, or vesicles. Anogenital ulcers specifically occur in the genital or anal regions and can be either painful or painless. It is important to note that a negative serological test for syphilis within three weeks of ulcer onset does not definitively rule out syphilis, as antibodies may not yet be detectable. Management of Anorectal Discharge 1. Molecular Testing in High-Resource Settings: For individuals with anorectal discharge who report receptive anal sex, WHO recommends using high-quality molecular assays (e.g., nucleic acid amplification tests or NAATs) to confirm or exclude infections with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and/or Chlamydia trachomatis. Treatment should be tailored to the specific infections detected. 2. Empirical Treatment in Low-Resource Settings: In settings where same-day molecular testing is not feasible, treatment should empirically cover N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis if discharge is present. If anorectal pain is reported, additional treatment for HSV should be considered. 3. Referral for Persistent Symptoms: Patients with persistent anorectal discharge should be referred to facilities with laboratory capacity to diagnose N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis (including lymphogranuloma venereum serovars), and Mycoplasma genitalium, as well as to assess antimicrobial resistance. Global Burden of STIs STIs remain a significant public health challenge worldwide, affecting physical, mental, and social well-being. They contribute to infertility, anogenital cancers, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and increased vulnerability to HIV transmission. Over one million curable STIs are acquired daily, with syphilis alone accounting for approximately three million new cases annually. The burden is highest in resource-limited countries, with the WHO African Region reporting the highest rates of gonorrhea and trichomoniasis, while the Region of the Americas has the highest rates of chlamydia and syphilis. Despite progress in preventing mother-to-child transmission of syphilis, congenital syphilis remains a concern, with an estimated 661,000 cases in 2016, including over 350,000 adverse birth outcomes such as stillbirths and neonatal deaths. Syndromic Management of STIs Syndromic management, introduced by WHO in 1984, remains a cornerstone of STI care in resource-limited settings. This approach uses clinical symptoms and signs to guide treatment without laboratory confirmation. While effective and cost-efficient, it has limitations, particularly in diagnosing cervical infections and managing antimicrobial resistance. Updated flowcharts for syndromic management are needed to address the changing epidemiology of STIs, including the predominance of HSV-2 as the leading cause of genital ulcer disease. Integration of STI and HIV Care HIV and other STIs often co-occur, requiring integrated approaches to prevention, testing, and treatment. Addressing stigma and discrimination in healthcare settings is critical to improving access to care and encouraging early diagnosis and treatment. Antimicrobial Resistance and Diagnostic Challenges Rising antimicrobial resistance in pathogens such as N. gonorrhoeae, T. pallidum, and M. genitalium underscores the need for updated treatment protocols that consider local and global resistance patterns. Near point-of-care molecular tests can provide same-visit results for gonorrhea and chlamydia, improving treatment outcomes and reducing delays in care. WHO Guidelines Development WHO has developed a phased approach to updating STI guidelines, focusing on evidence-based recommendations for managing symptomatic STIs, preventing infections, and addressing antimicrobial resistance. These guidelines aim to improve access to high-quality STI care, particularly in resource-limited settings, while promoting human rights and gender equity. Conclusion The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based, integrated, and patient-centered approaches to STI prevention and management. By addressing diagnostic challenges, antimicrobial resistance, and the syndemics of HIV and STIs, these guidelines aim to reduce the global burden of STIs and improve sexual health outcomes worldwide.
